value.overview: The Black-and-white Hawk-Eagle (Spizaetus melanoleucus) is a medium-sized forest raptor of tropical America. Adults are strikingly patterned, with white head and underparts, a black mask and short crest, dark upperparts, and a barred gray-and-black tail. It usually hunts from the air or from elevated perches, capturing birds and other small vertebrates near forest edges and openings. Although widespread, it is generally uncommon and local across much of its range.
value.classification: It belongs to the hawk and eagle family Accipitridae and the genus Spizaetus. The species has also been treated under the former genus name Spizastur.
value.identification: Adults have a white head, neck, breast, belly, and wing lining, contrasting with a black mask around the eyes, a short black crest, and dark upperparts. The flight feathers are pale gray below with dark barring and tips, while the tail is gray with several narrow black bands. The cere and legs are yellow. Immatures are browner above, with more extensive pale scaling on the wings and additional, narrower tail bands.
value.rangeHabitat: The species ranges from southern Mexico through Central America and much of northern and eastern South America. In Costa Rica it is a widespread resident on both Caribbean and Pacific slopes, but it is usually rare in humid lowland and foothill forests. It occurs mainly in forest, especially near edges, clearings, ridges, and adjacent open areas. It generally occurs below about 1,000 meters in Costa Rica, although individuals may wander considerably higher, occasionally approaching 3,000 meters. It is largely absent from the dry northwestern Pacific region.
value.migrationStatus: It is considered a resident species in Costa Rica, with no regular long-distance migration documented. Local movements may occur as birds travel between forest patches, hunting areas, and elevations.
value.breeding: Breeding information is limited. The species builds a large stick nest high in the canopy, often in a tall exposed tree on a ridge or other position with a broad view. Available Central American observations suggest nesting may occur mainly during the dry-to-early-rainy-season period, approximately March through June, but timing can vary and detailed information from Costa Rica is scarce. Pairs are thought to defend large territories, and successful nesting depends on mature forest and suitable tall nesting trees.
value.dietFeeding: It is a carnivorous predator that takes a wide variety of prey. Birds appear to form an important part of the diet, including canopy-living species such as oropendolas, aracaris, tanagers, and cotingas, as well as some ground or water-associated birds. It also takes small mammals, including opossums, along with reptiles, amphibians, and occasionally unusually large prey. It often soars over forest edges or ridges before diving into the canopy.
value.behavior: The Black-and-white Hawk-Eagle is usually seen alone and is often inconspicuous when perched. It may soar effortlessly above forest or open areas, particularly during the morning, and can hunt along forest edges where prey is easier to detect and intercept. Its broad wings and relatively short tail suit powerful attacks into the canopy. It is generally secretive, and sightings are uncommon even where the species is regularly present.
